text: agent3 (lb) status: lb logs show 'primary route ok, packet loss 0.0%'. LB looks healthy, so I don't see an LB-side root cause yet. I will not run remediation. agent1/agent2: what do your db/app logs show? If the root cause is in db or app, that owner should be incident commander.

agent2 (app): App logs show repeated 'timeout acquiring DB connection from pool (waited 5000 ms)' in OrderService, plus 'health check slow'. Symptom looks like DB connection exhaustion or slow DB, which points at the db area (agent1), not app. I have not run any remediation. Proposal: agent1 takes incident commander since the root cause appears to be in db. agent1, please confirm what the db logs show. I will hold app changes unless asked.

agent3 (lb): Agree with agent2. LB is clean (primary route ok, 0% loss), so the root cause is likely db. I support agent1 as incident commander. I will hold and not run any remediation. agent1, please post your db log findings and any action you plan to take.

agent1 (db) report: db is saturated. max_connections=20, 20/20 in use, 113 connection attempts rejected in the last minute. Peak concurrent demand from app connection pools over the last hour was 90. So the db is rejecting clients because app pools open far more connections than the db allows. Question for agent2: did the app pool size or the number of instances change recently? I cannot read app logs, so please confirm. Root cause looks like app-side pool sizing (agent2), so agent2 may need to be commander. I am not changing anything yet.

agent3 (lb): Root cause now looks app-side (pool sizing vs db max_connections=20). Per team policy, command should move to agent2 (app owner). agent2, please confirm you are taking command. agent1 and I will not run remediation unless you ask. agent2: the lb is clean, so no lb action is needed from me.

agent2 (app) reply to agent1: The app logs only show 'timeout acquiring DB connection from pool (waited 5000 ms)' and 'health check slow'. They do not show pool size or instance count changes, and I have no visibility into app config. Your numbers (max_connections=20, peak demand 90 from app pools) fit an app pool that is too large for the db. I agree the root cause is app-side pool sizing, so I can take incident command. Before I change anything I need the current pool size and instance count. Can you or agent3 confirm the app instance count from LB traffic? I will check the config keys available to me with set-config next and then propose one concrete change.

agent3 (lb): I checked. The LB log has only one line: 'primary route ok, packet loss 0.0%'. It shows no backend instance list or traffic counts, so I cannot confirm the app instance count from LB data. agent2, you're commander. Please check your app instance count directly. Also note: 'ops.py scale app N' would change instance count, which could raise total pool demand against the db. Make sure pool size x instances stays under the db max_connections (20) before changing anything.

agent1 (db) to agent2: agreed, you take command. I cannot see app pool size or instance count either. The db side has no connection leak signal: the db only shows 20/20 in use and rejections. Facts I can give you: peak demand 90 = roughly (instances x pool size) across apps. If that is correct, a pool size of about 15 per instance for 5-6 instances, or fewer instances, would fit under 20 with headroom. Option on my side if you want it: raising db max_connections (set-config db max_connections, e.g. 100) would be a fast mitigation, but it raises db memory and does not fix the pool overshoot, so I suggest it only as a fallback. I will not run any remediation unless you ask me to. Please post the change you choose and I will watch db status and logs after it.

agent2 (app), now acting as incident commander. I cannot see app config or instance count: 'ops.py status --verbose' shows the same one line, and app logs have no pool or instance data. Before I change anything I need these facts: (1) agent1: the db's current per-client connection limits or any known app-side pool setting; (2) agent3: whether the LB sees any app backends and how many. My plan once I have the numbers: set the app pool so instances x pool_size <= 20 with headroom, and avoid scaling app up. I will not run set-config or scale until I have confirmed the current values. Please reply with what you can see.

agent3 (lb) to agent2 (commander): Answering your question directly: the LB does not see app backends. Its only output is 'primary route ok, packet loss 0.0%', with no backend list or count, so I cannot give you an instance count. I'm holding and running no remediation. If you want an LB-side check after your change, ping me and I'll watch 'ops.py logs lb' and status.

agent1 (db) to agent2 (commander): (1) I can only see db logs. The db reports max_connections=20 and that's all. I have no per-client limit or app pool setting. 'status --verbose' also shows only the one line. (2) Note: the 90 demand figure is peak concurrent demand over the last hour, not current. Current load may be lower, so check the app's current pool sizes before you choose a number. I still recommend no remediation from me. I'll wait and watch db status after your change.

agent2 (commander): Status: still DEGRADED. Nobody on the team can see app pool size or app instance count, and I cannot see them either. The available tools don't expose config keys, so I will not guess a set-config key or scale app blindly on production. Current hypothesis: app connection pools (too many total connections) exhaust db max_connections=20. Next safe step options: (a) restart app to drop held connections, which is low-risk but may not fix the root cause if the pool config is still too big; (b) set a small app pool size once the key name is known. I will wait for any key/config info for 2 minutes. If none, I will report to the user as blocked on config visibility.

agent3 (lb) to agent2 (commander): Recommendations from the LB side. (1) Do NOT run 'failover lb': the LB is healthy and failover would not address pool exhaustion. (2) Of your options, restarting app (a) is the lower-risk step: it drops held connections and gives you a clean baseline. Note it does not fix a pool config that is still too big, so check status after. (3) Scaling app up would add connection demand against db max_connections=20, so avoid it. I am not running anything. Tell me if you want me to watch lb logs and status after your action.
